entry.title: A Better Shop Floor Starts Now
entry.content:
Part 1 and part 2 were largely about the strategic decisions at board level and the technical decisions in the architecture room. This final part is about something rather more immediate than either of those.

It is about the person who walks into the plant at six in the morning, checks how the overnight production run went, and starts their day with whatever the current system happens to give them. Sometimes that is enough to work with, but often it is not, and the workarounds that have grown up to fill the gap have become so familiar that most teams have simply stopped noticing they are there.

That is the part of this whole transition that does not get talked about nearly enough. It is not the architecture or the timeline that ultimately determines whether this change is worth making, it is the day-to-day experience of the people running production.

The tools have not kept up

SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence and SAP Manufacturing Execution were built on technology that is now well over twenty years old, and in manufacturing terms that is a genuinely significant gap. The shop floors these platforms were originally designed for looked quite different from today’s, the expectations placed on operations teams were different, and the speed at which decisions needed to be made was different again.

What has not changed, oddly enough, is the expectation that the people running production will somehow bridge the distance between what the system shows them and what is happening on the floor in front of them. End-of-shift data consolidation, manual re-entry between systems, quality checks logged after the fact rather than embedded into the process itself, dashboards that finally become accurate at roughly the same moment nobody needs them anymore and these are the everyday realities that operations teams have quietly absorbed for years.

None of this reflects a failure of process or effort on the part of the people involved. These are limitations of the platform itself, and they carry a cost that rarely gets properly quantified precisely because it has become background noise that nobody thinks to measure.

What actually changes

SAP Digital Manufacturing is built around a fairly straightforward premise: the people running manufacturing operations should have the information they need at the moment they need it, without having to go looking for it. That sounds simple enough on paper, but the implications of actually delivering on it are considerable.

Production visibility shifts from retrospective to genuinely near live. Dashboards update in near real time, but increasingly the experience is also becoming conversational. With SAP's AI capabilities and Joule, supervisors and production teams can interact with manufacturing information more naturally, helping them identify issues, understand performance trends, and access relevant operational insights faster. Anyone with responsibility for what is happening on the floor can see the current state of production orders, work center status, and material availability without waiting for someone to compile a report.

Work instructions become part of the process itself rather than a document that lives somewhere alongside it. The process designer in SAP Digital Manufacturing delivers digital work instructions including images and video where they help directly to the operator at the point of execution. That matters for quality, for onboarding new operators, and for keeping things consistent across shifts, because the instruction and the step it applies to now exist in the same place at the same time.

Another important shift is the increasing integration between production equipment and manufacturing processes. In many environments, machines can receive production-related information directly from SAP Digital Manufacturing and return execution data, process parameters, and production results back into the process record. Operators remain at the center of execution, but they no longer need to manually capture every piece of information required for traceability. The result is a more complete digital history of how products were manufactured, greater process transparency, and faster access to the information needed for quality, compliance, and continuous improvement.

Quality stops being a downstream activity that happens after the fact. In-process quality inspections get embedded directly into production steps, triggered automatically, with the results flowing to SAP S/4HANA Quality Management in real time. The practical effect is that the quality team spends less time chasing data around and more time actually acting on it.

OEE becomes a tool rather than a report. Overall Equipment Effectiveness tracking is built in, downtime events get classified, and performance trends surface without anyone having to manually pull them together. When a line stops, the system already knows, and when a pattern starts to emerge over time, it becomes easier to identify recurring causes and address them before they have a broader operational impact. Operational visibility improves not only within production itself, but also across the wider manufacturing landscape.

The gap between the shop floor and the ERP system essentially closes. The result is not only better synchronization between systems. It is a closer connection between manufacturing operations and the broader business, helping teams make decisions based on the same information, priorities, and customer commitments.

Production order confirmations, goods movements, inventory postings, and quality results all move between SAP Digital Manufacturing and SAP S/4HANA automatically, which means the synchronization delays and manual re-entry that have historically sat between the plant, and the wider business simply go away.

The transition itself

A fair question at this point is what the changeover actually feels like for the people going through it, and the honest answer is that it takes some adjustment. Workflows that have been second nature for years will genuinely work differently in the new environment, and any transition program that pretends otherwise is not really serving its people well.

What makes the difference is how that change is managed, rather than whether the platform itself is any good. SAP and its partner ecosystem have built enablement programs specifically aimed at operations teams making this kind of move, and the ones that matter most in practice tend to be role-based learning paths through SAP Learning Hub structured around the work that production supervisors, quality engineers, planners, and operators actually do rather than around generic system training along with proper process simulation before go-live so that teams are not encountering the new system for the first time on the day it matters most, and dedicated hyper-care support in the weeks immediately after go-live to resolve questions quickly and keep adoption moving forward.

The goal of a well-run transition is that day one in SAP Digital Manufacturing feels manageable rather than overwhelming, and that outcome is genuinely achievable, but it requires the investment in people to be treated with the same seriousness as the investment in the technology itself.

A Platform that does not stand still

One of the more meaningful differences between SAP Digital Manufacturing and what it is replacing is harder to put on a feature list, because it is really about trajectory rather than any specific capability

Legacy SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence and SAP Manufacturing Execution platforms are at the end of their development lifecycle. What they are today is essentially what they will be in 2027, because no new capabilities are coming, no new integrations are being built, and there is no roadmap ahead of them.

SAP Digital Manufacturing sits on the opposite side of that equation. It is a cloud product with an active development program, and its capabilities improve on a continuous release cycle without any of the upgrade projects that used to accompany that kind of change. What the platform can do in 2026 will be materially more than what it does today, and more again the year after that.

The roadmap continues to evolve with new capabilities across areas such as planning, quality, sustainability, asset performance, and traceability. The specific features matter, but the bigger point is that the platform continues to improve without the disruption of traditional upgrade projects.

The point is that operations teams working on SAP Digital Manufacturing are not just getting a better platform today. They are getting one that keeps getting better on its own, automatically, as part of the service they are already paying for.

Getting the transition right on the ground

Technology transitions ultimately succeed or fail at the operational level. The architecture can be perfectly sound and the project management admirably disciplined, but if the people closest to the process are not properly involved from the beginning, the gap between what was designed and what actually gets used tends to widen surprisingly quickly after go-live.

Three things consistently make the difference in my experience. The first is capturing how the floor runs before design work begins, every workaround, every informal step, every little process that has grown up outside the system over the years. That knowledge is rarely obvious to program teams arriving from the outside, and it is exactly the kind of thing that good system design needs to reflect if it is going to work in practice.

The second is identifying what really matters before the build starts, particularly the reports, dashboards, and KPIs that production and quality teams rely on every day. If these are not properly validated before go-live, the first few weeks on the new platform end up being spent rebuilding trust rather than building capability, which is not a position anyone wants to find themselves in.

The third is getting into the system early. Simulation and training opportunities are available well before go-live, and the teams that actually make use of them rather than waiting for formal training closer to the date arrive at cutover with genuine familiarity rather than surface-level awareness. That difference is visible on day one, and it tends to compound from there.

The bigger picture

Across all three parts of this series, the argument has been fairly consistent. The end of SAP NetWeaver’s mainstream maintenance is not an inconvenience to be managed and moved past but it is a defined moment to make a deliberate choice about what kind of manufacturing organization you intend to be on the other side of it.

Part 1 made the case for moving with intent rather than out of obligation. Part 2 laid out how a well-structured technical program actually comes together. Part 3 is really just the reminder that both of those things ultimately serve one purpose, which is giving the people running manufacturing operations better tools, better information, and a platform capable of keeping pace with where the industry is heading. Better manufacturing systems ultimately matter because they help organizations deliver consistently on the promises they make to customers, whether that means quality, delivery performance, compliance, or responsiveness.

That is what this transition is genuinely about.

Not a deadline, and certainly not a compliance checkbox, but an opportunity to build a better shop floor and a stronger manufacturing organization while there is still time to do it deliberately and do it well.

entry.title: What SAP Process Integration/Process Orchestration Customers Need to Know About the 2030 Timeline
entry.content:
SAP recently published guidance covering the implications of the 2030 maintenance timeline for SAP Business Suite 7 and SAP NetWeaver customers. If you are running SAP Process Orchestration (PO) or SAP Process Integration (PI) — even if you have already moved off SAP ERP or SAP Business Suite 7 — this article is relevant to you.

Why This Matters for PI/PO Customers

SAP Process Orchestration and SAP Process Integration are built on SAP NetWeaver Application Server 7.5 for Java (NW AS Java). As outlined in the guidance, SAP's current support arrangements for Java used with NW AS Java 7.5 are scheduled to conclude at the end of 2030. This constraint applies to PI/PO independently of whether you are also running SAP Business Suite 7.

To state this precisely:

  • Mainstream maintenance for SAP Process Orchestration 7.5: ends December 31, 2027
  • Optional extended maintenance: runs through December 31, 2030
  • After 2030: customer-specific maintenance (CSM) — without a follow-on release.
  • For SAP Process Orchestration, Private Cloud Edition (PO PCE): maintenance ends December 31, 2030. Refer to SAP Note 3833114.

Entering customer-specific maintenance (CSM) without a follow-on release goes beyond a standard end-of-maintenance message. At the end of 2030, SAP's support arrangements for Java used with NW AS Java 7.5 shall expire,. After this point, SAP will not be able to provide comprehensive support for Java or database-related issues in these environments. This makes CSM an unsustainable long-term model for business-critical integration infrastructure.

The Path Forward

SAP Integration Suite is SAP's strategic integration platform, trusted by enterprises worldwide to support all integration patterns while enabling customers to scale, secure, and govern their holistic integration landscape. SAP has invested extensively to help ensure SAP Integration Suite supports all current integration patterns while future-proofing your integration landscape — delivering AI-ready capabilities that enable you to connect AI agents, create intelligent processes that are reliable, secure and can scale, and govern your modern enterprise-wide digital ecosystem with confidence.

Whether your focus is on connecting hybrid landscapes, accelerating AI-driven automation, enabling API and event-driven architectures, connecting with business partners through industry-specific B2B standards, or aligning with a clean core approach, consider SAP Integration Suite is designed to support all these needs. We have made it our mission to make your transition with minimal disruption and maximal value for your future landscapes

entry.title: SAP NetWeaver 7.5 SP35 Upgrade: JDBC DataSources Unavailable Due to TLS Protocol Changes
entry.content:
Issue and Error Analysis

The affected custom DataSources included SAPMEINT, SAPMEINTXA, SAPMEWIP, dmPool, odsDiagPool, odsPool, reportPool, and wipPool.

When attempting to start a DataSource, the NetWeaver logs reported the following error:

The driver could not establish a secure connection to SQL Server
by using Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) encryption.

Error: "No appropriate protocol
(protocol is disabled or cipher suites are inappropriate)".

The error indicated a failure during secure communication between the SAP NetWeaver Java stack and Microsoft SQL Server.

Root Cause

The investigation led us to SAP Note 3046818, which documents changes introduced in SAP JVM 8.1 Patch Collection 74 (build 8.1.074).

As part of these changes, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are disabled by default.

Our environment was using the legacy Microsoft SQL Server JDBC Driver 4.0 (sqljdbc4.jar). The updated JVM security policy caused a TLS compatibility issue with the existing database connectivity configuration, resulting in the failure of all affected DataSources.

Resolution

We resolved the issue by updating the SAP JVM security configuration as described in SAP Note 3046818.

The following steps were performed:

  1. Located the java.security file in the active SAP JVM installation.
  2. Modified the jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms property by removing TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 from the disabled protocols list, as described in the SAP Note.
  3. Restarted the SAP system to apply the updated JVM security configuration.
  4. Validated the JDBC Custom DataSources in NetWeaver Administrator.
  5. Confirmed that the affected DataSources were available and verified the functionality of the ME application, including the CTC task.

Following these changes, the JDBC connectivity issue was resolved.

Security consideration: Re-enabling TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is a compatibility workaround, not the preferred long-term solution. These protocols are obsolete. Where feasible, evaluate a supported JDBC driver and database configuration that allow TLS 1.2 to be used without relaxing the JVM security policy.

Key Takeaways

This incident highlights the importance of reviewing SAP JVM security changes during SAP NetWeaver upgrades.

Even when an upgrade completes successfully, changes to default security settings can affect existing integrations and database connectivity.

For future SAP ME/MII upgrades, we recommend:

  • Reviewing SAP JVM patch-level changes and relevant SAP Notes.
  • Verifying JDBC driver compatibility with the target Java runtime and SQL Server TLS configuration.
  • Validating all critical JDBC DataSources immediately after the upgrade.
  • Including the required system restart and application-level validation in the upgrade checklist.

References

  • SAP Note 3046818

entry.title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones.

The configuration covered here implements TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store, allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

Prerequisites

  • Database certificate (.pfx format) signed by an external CA, plus the corresponding root certificate
  • Certificate password
  • Access to the HANA database server at OS level (sidadm or equivalent)
  • Access to all ABAP application server nodes at OS level
  • A valid HANA userstore key configured for hdbsql commands
  • Planned downtime or maintenance window — the ABAP application must be stopped during parts of this procedure
  • Existing SAPSSLS.pse backed up before making any changes

Overview

The procedure creates two sets of PSE (Personal Security Environment) files:

  1. SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA server — the HANA database server's SSL identity, built from the externally signed certificate. This is what HANA presents to the ABAP layer during the TLS handshake.

  2. sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse on each ABAP application server — these are placed in the sec directory of each ABAP node. They act as the trust store on the ABAP side, containing the CA certificate chain that the ABAP kernel uses to verify HANA's certificate. The sslKeyStore reference in the profile parameter also points to sapcli.pse, but since sslclientpki is off on HANA, the client certificate is never requested.

Step 1 — Upload Certificates to the HANA Server

  1. Log on to the HANA database server at OS level as sidadm
  2. Upload the database certificate (db_cert.pfx), the root certificate (root.cer) (and any intermediate certificates) to the sec directory on the HANA server:
/usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/global/security/rsecssls/

Note: The exact sec directory path may vary. Confirm the location using the SECUDIR environment variable.

  1. Before making any changes, back up the existing SAPSSLS.pse:
cp SAPSSLS.pse SAPSSLS.pse.bak

Step 2 — Create SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA Server

Run the following command to create a new SAPSSLS.pse from the externally signed certificate. This becomes the HANA server's SSL identity:

sapgenpse import_p12 -r root.cer -p SAPSSLS.pse <db_cert.pfx>
  • Enter the certificate password when prompted
  • When asked for a PIN, you have the option to set one or leave it empty. From a security perspective, setting a PIN is recommended as it adds an additional layer of protection to the PSE file. If a PIN is set, ensure it is stored securely as it will be required for any future PSE operations

SAPSSLS.pse should now be created successfully.

Step 3 — Create the Client PSE Files for ABAP Application Servers

sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse can be created directly from SAPSSLS.pse:

cp SAPSSLS.pse sapcli.pse
cp SAPSSLS.pse sapsrv.pse

Copy both files to the sec directory on every ABAP application server node (CS/CI and all additional application servers):

/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/

Step 4 — Disable sslclientpki on HANA

Important: Shut down the ABAP application layer before executing this step.

This parameter controls whether HANA enforces client PKI certificate authentication. Setting it to off enables one-way TLS (server authentication only), which is the configuration used here.

Run the following hdbsql command from the HANA server:

hdbsql -U <USERSTORE_KEY> "ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') SET ('communication', 'sslclientpki') = 'off' WITH RECONFIGURE;"

The WITH RECONFIGURE clause applies the change immediately without requiring a HANA restart.

PRD Systems: This parameter must also be disabled on the secondary/DR HANA node. This can be done via SAP HANA Studio — apply the change on both the primary and DR secondary database nodes.

Step 5 — Configure the ABAP Default Profile

The dbs/hdb/connect_property parameter must be added to the ABAP default profile (DEFAULT.PFL) to instruct the ABAP kernel to use SSL when connecting to HANA. This parameter applies to all application server instances.

Add the following parameter (adapt values to your system):

dbs/hdb/connect_property = ENCRYPT=TRUE,sslCryptoProvider=commoncrypto,sslKeyStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslTrustStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslHostNameInCertificate=<hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com>

Key values to adapt:

  • <SID> — your system ID
  • <instance_dir> — the instance directory of each application server (e.g. D00, D01)
  • <hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com> — the fully qualified hostname as it appears in the HANA certificate's CN/SAN field

Note: The sslHostNameInCertificate value must match exactly what is embedded in the HANA server certificate, otherwise the SSL handshake will fail.

Step 6 — Restart the Application and Validate

Start the ABAP application layer. Once all instances are up, perform the following validation steps.

Validation 1 — Check encrypted connections via SQL

Log on to the system and navigate to transaction DB02 → SQL Editor. Run the following statement, replacing <SCHEMA> with the correct database schema name:

SELECT IS_ENCRYPTED, SSL_VERSION, CLIENT_HOST
FROM SYS.M_CONNECTIONS
WHERE USER_NAME = '<SCHEMA>'
AND IS_ENCRYPTED = 'TRUE';

All active connections for the schema should return TRUE in the IS_ENCRYPTED column. If any sessions return FALSE, review the profile parameter and PSE file placement.

Validation 2 — R3trans connectivity check

Run the following from the OS level on each application server to confirm no transport-layer issues:

R3trans -d

Review the trans.log output — a clean run with no errors confirms successful connectivity between the ABAP application layer and HANA over SSL.

Summary

At this point, SSL encryption between the SAP ABAP application servers and SAP HANA is active using an externally signed CA certificate. The HANA server authenticates to the application layer via SAPSSLS.pse, while each ABAP node uses sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse as its trust store for verifying HANA's identity.

This guide was produced by the IT Planning and Software Logistics team, SAP Ireland, based on field experience from enterprise RISE migration projects.
